summary.text: Star formation is the process in which dense regions inside molecular clouds collapse and form stars.
A cloud collapses under its own gravity when it is massive enough that its gas pressure cannot support it, above a mass called the Jeans mass.
Most stars do not form alone but as part of a group of stars called a star cluster or a stellar association.

items.prompt: A cloud of gas floats in space, held steady by two opposing effects. What would have to be true for it to fall inward and begin making stars?

options.label: Its mass would have to be so large that the push of its gas can no longer support it
It would have to cool until all of its gas is perfectly still
It would have to spin fast enough to flatten into a pancake
It would have to be heated until its gas glows brightly

items.explain: A cloud stays in balance while gas pressure and gravity match. If a cloud is massive enough that the gas pressure is insufficient, it collapses.

items.prompt: Two clouds of gas share the same temperature and density, but one is far heavier. Only one is likely to collapse by itself. Which one?

options.label: The lighter one, since a small cloud has more room to shrink
Both, since a cloud this cold always falls inward
The heavier one, since it exceeds the mass where gas pressure fails to hold a cloud up
Neither, since a cloud never falls inward without outside help

items.explain: A cloud collapses once its mass is above the Jeans mass, which depends on temperature and density.

items.prompt: An astronomer spots one brand-new star. Based on how stars usually form, what should she expect to find nearby?

options.label: An empty region, since collapse pushes neighbours away
Other young stars, since most stars form in groups
A single bigger star that it will soon swallow
Only dust, since stars form strictly one at a time

items.explain: Most stars do not form in isolation but as part of star clusters or stellar associations.

items.prompt: As a gas cloud collapses it keeps breaking into smaller pieces, yet the splitting eventually stops. What brings it to a halt?

options.label: Magnetic fields lock the pieces tightly together
A black hole at the center pulls the pieces back
The pieces turn opaque, shed heat poorly, and warm up
The pieces run out of hydrogen and fall apart

items.explain: As density rises, fragments become opaque and less efficient at radiating energy away, which raises the temperature and inhibits further fragmentation.

items.prompt: A weaker jet from a galaxy's central black hole slams into a cloud of gas. What might that do for the cloud?

options.label: It might help push the cloud into forming stars
It always blows the cloud apart for good
It turns the cloud into a small galaxy
Nothing, because jets and clouds never interact

items.explain: A weaker jet may trigger star formation when it collides with a cloud, although a strong active jet can limit it.

items.prompt: Astronomers compare the coldest clouds with the generally warmer giant ones. Which statement fits?

options.label: The coldest make only massive stars, and the warmer giants make only small ones
The coldest tend to make small stars, while the warmer giants make stars of all sizes
The coldest make no stars, and only the warmer giants do
Both kinds make stars of exactly one size

items.explain: The coldest clouds tend to form low-mass stars, while giant molecular clouds, which are generally warmer, produce stars of all masses.

beats.title: How clouds collapse into stars
beats.hook: A cloud of gas stays in balance until one thing tips it into collapse.

beats.prompt: A cloud's gas pressure balances its gravity. Then enough mass builds up that the pressure can no longer support it. What happens?
beats.explain: If a cloud is massive enough that the gas pressure is insufficient to support it, it undergoes gravitational collapse.

choices.label: It settles into a calmer balance
choices.feedback: Balance is exactly what is lost once the gas pressure is insufficient to support the cloud.

choices.label: It spreads out and thins away
choices.feedback: Thinning away would need pressure to win, but here gravity is the stronger side.

beats.prompt: Sort each black-hole effect by what it can do to star formation.

left.label: An active black hole's strong wind and jet
Near-light-speed particles blocking new stars in aging galaxies
A weaker jet colliding with a cloud

beats.explain: Strong output from an accreting black hole can limit star formation, while weaker jets and radio emissions may trigger it.

beats.prompt: Put these steps of a collapsing cloud in order.

items.label: The cloud breaks into smaller and smaller pieces
The collapsing gas radiates away the energy gained
As density increases, the fragments become opaque
The cloud warms and further splitting is inhibited

beats.explain: As density rises the fragments turn opaque and radiate less efficiently, which raises the temperature and inhibits further fragmentation.

paragraphs.heading: How stars are born
paragraphs.text: Star formation is the process in which dense parts of molecular clouds collapse and become stars. These star-making regions are sometimes called stellar nurseries. Spiral galaxies such as the Milky Way contain stars, stellar remnants, and a thin, spread-out mix of gas and dust called the interstellar medium (ISM). The study of star formation looks at the ISM and giant molecular clouds as the raw material, and at protostars and young stellar objects as the result.

paragraphs.heading: The raw material
paragraphs.text: By mass, the interstellar medium is usually about 70% hydrogen, 28% helium and 1.5% heavier elements. Those heavier elements were made inside stars and thrown out as the stars passed the end of their main sequence lifetime. Denser regions of the medium form clouds, or diffuse nebulae, and these are where stars form. In the dense nebulae that make stars, much of the hydrogen is in molecules (H₂), so they are called molecular clouds.

paragraphs.heading: Giant molecular clouds
paragraphs.text: Giant molecular clouds typically have about 100 particles per cubic centimetre, are about 100 light-years across, and can hold up to six million times the mass of the Sun. Their average inside temperature is 10 K. About half the mass of the Milky Way's interstellar medium sits in molecular clouds, and the galaxy has an estimated 6,000 that are each more than 100,000 solar masses. The coldest clouds tend to form low-mass stars, while giant molecular clouds, which are generally warmer, make stars of all masses.

paragraphs.heading: Why a cloud collapses
paragraphs.text: A cloud of gas stays in balance, called hydrostatic equilibrium, as long as the energy of its gas pressure matches the pull of its own gravity. The virial theorem states this in numbers: to stay balanced, gravitational potential energy has to be double the internal thermal energy. If a cloud is so massive that its gas pressure cannot hold it up, it collapses under gravity. The Jeans mass, the mass above which this happens, depends on the cloud's temperature and density and usually lies somewhere between thousands and tens of thousands of solar masses.

paragraphs.heading: From threads to stars
paragraphs.text: The Herschel Space Observatory showed that filaments, long dense structures of gas, are everywhere in molecular clouds and central to forming stars. They break up into cores held together by gravity, and most of those cores will become stars. As a cloud collapses it splits into smaller and smaller pieces until the pieces reach the mass of a star. Each piece gets denser until it becomes opaque and can no longer shed its energy well, so it heats up and stops splitting.

paragraphs.heading: Born in crowds
paragraphs.text: Most stars form not alone but in groups. When a cloud collapses, dozens to tens of thousands of stars form at about the same time, which can be seen in embedded clusters, and the end product is an open cluster. The nearest nebula to the Sun where massive stars are forming is the Orion Nebula, 1,300 light-years away. Smaller sites are Bok globules, opaque clouds of dense gas and dust typically up to a light-year across, and over half of the known ones hold newly forming stars.

paragraphs.heading: Black holes as brakes and triggers
paragraphs.text: A supermassive black hole at the centre of a galaxy may help set how fast stars form there. A black hole that is swallowing infalling matter can become active and blow out a strong wind through a narrow jet, and this can limit further star formation. Yet the radio emission around such jets may also trigger star formation, and so may a weaker jet when it hits a cloud.
